RagShortTexts: The rise of the Zenata Berber Marinid Dynasty in Fez transformed cross-Strait Iberian politics.

Variants.Content: By 1259 the Almohad Caliphate had lost most of its power. The Marinids had taken Fez in 1248 and dominated the north, while the Almohads still held Marrakesh until 1269. The Marinids rose from Zenata Berber pastoral tribes, so their strength rested on mounted levies that could be called up quickly and moved across the Rif and Atlas passes. Their army leaned on light cavalry and javelin throwers rather than heavy armour, which suited hill country and mountain tracks. In Granada, the Nasrid court watched this rise with mixed hope and unease: a strong Marinid state across the Strait could check Castile, yet it could also turn the Strait into a route for an army answering to Fez.

Fez now decides whether the Strait of Gibraltar stays a frontier or becomes a highway for invasion. Every Castilian lord on the Andalusian coast reckons the cost of galleys, garrisons and grain for Tarifa, because a single Marinid landing could cut the southern cities off from their supply lines. Diplomacy with Granada and the Marinid court therefore weighs as heavily as any fortress wall.

The Marinid riders are wiry men on Barb horses ridden bareback, carrying javelins that they throw with either hand. When the easterly wind holds across the Strait, their raids can strike the southern beaches in a single night. Hold your footing carefully on wet sand, because the raiders know every dune and will be gone before the watch can form a line.
